LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Notice, Understand, Comfort & Encourage — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches empathy as a walkable path with four steps — because noticing someone’s feelings is a skill, and like every skill it can be practised by a four-year-old.

What is this?

Notice, understand, comfort and encourage are the four empathy steps: notice catches the feeling on someone’s face, understand works out why, comfort softens the hurt and encourage hands them courage for the next try.

What does it mean?

Empathy is usually described as a feeling, but for children it is a procedure — four small moves in order. Children who know the moves run them on friends, pets and parents, and the running changes them.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: feelings show on FACES and BODIES (the noticing); the best question is "are you… because…?" (the understanding); and comfort can be quiet — a sit-together is a full sentence.

Why this matters

This card is the class’s kindness engine: every later people-word — support, care, comfort, include — uses these four steps. Run them here on toys and teddies first, where mistakes are free.

What it teaches

Perspective-taking (the cognitive heart of empathy), emotion recognition in others, helping behaviour, and emotional first aid — the child-sized version of what nurses call a good bedside manner.

Words to learn

noticeunderstandcomfortencourageempathyfeelingshelp

Say this to your child

“"When someone is sad, our heart wants to help — but HOW? Four steps. First, notice: look at their face. Sad eyebrows? Dropped shoulders? Second, understand: ask gently — are you sad because…? Third, comfort: a hug, a hand, or just sitting close — comfort can be quiet. Fourth, encourage: when they are ready, the cheer — try again, I am right here. Eyes, question, hug, cheer. That is how you help a heart — and hearts remember everyone who helped."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four steps for helping a heart."
  2. Walk the panels: the hand-raised boy NOTICES, the chin-thinking girl UNDERSTANDS, the heart-hugging boy COMFORTS, the fist-up girl ENCOURAGES.
  3. Drill the sequence on a teddy with a problem (lost button, scary dream): your child runs all four steps out loud — "I notice you look sad… do you feel sad because the button is gone?… come here, I will sit with you… you can find it, I will help."
  4. Swap: the grown-up runs the steps for YOUR child’s small real wobble, naming each step as you take it.
  5. Close with the rescue game below and the takeaway: "first the eyes, then the question, then the hug, then the cheer."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels show the steps: Notice, an attentive boy with his hand raised; Understand, a girl nodding with a finger to her chin; Comfort, a boy hugging a pink heart; and Encourage, a girl cheering with a fist up — the helping sequence exactly as a child runs it.

Ask your child

"What is step one — eyes or hugs?" "What question helps us understand?" "Can comfort be quiet?" "What does encourage sound like?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I noticed my friend was sad!" "Are you sad because…?" (the full formula) or the tender one: "I sat with him until he felt better."

Out in the real world

Rescue missions appear all day: a sibling’s dropped ice cream, a friend’s skinned knee at the park, the dog hiding from the vacuum, a parent losing their keys. Run the four steps on small scale emergencies — the practice is the point, not the fix.

Try it together

Feelings Rescue Patrol: one stuffed animal per round "needs help" (a broken wheel, a lost spot, a scary noise). Your child is the rescue patrol and must run all four steps before the rescue is complete — the animal’s face must go from sad to cheered. Four rescues, four full sequences, one empathic pro.

Understanding check

Ask: "What comes after noticing? Can comfort be quiet? What does encourage do?" Understanding, yes, cheers — three answers and the empathy steps are in service.

Parent tips

Resist fixing fast — the understand step needs the question, not the solution, and children skip it because grown-ups model skipping it. Slow down deliberately: "I notice your face looks disappointed… was it because…?" And praise the noticing loudest of all: eyes that catch feelings are the rarest part.

This lesson pairs with the Notice, Understand, Comfort & Encourage flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).
